utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom. The witness should be brought in, please. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, while we wait for the witness, I wanted to raise a brief issue. Exhibit P2251. There are actually two exhibits that have been assigned the same number which is P2251. Namely, 65 ter 4088 by the OTP; and 2240. They were both placed under the same number in two different locations. Could we please deal with that so that both of them would have different numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this information, Mr. Gajic. Mr. Registrar will check that and he just confirmed to me that you are right. And it will be put on the record the relevant correction. Good afternoon, sir. Welcome back to the courtroom. I have to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth you made at the beginning of your testimony still applies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer is continuing his examination-in-chief. You have the floor, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon to you and Your Honours. Good afternoon to the Defence. Good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And good afternoon to you, Mr. Mitrovic. When we left off yesterday, sir, you were in the process of describing for us the general structure an operation of the Eastern Bosnia Corps Commission for the Exchange of Prisoners of War. Did part of the commission's work also include the exchange of the mortal remains of soldiers from both sides of the conflict, or were you occupied solely with living prisoners?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were also involved in exchanging the bodies of fallen soldiers, as well as in exchanging of POWs.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And was the process with respect to repatriating those remains, obtaining those remains, basically the same as that of exchanging living prisoners?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We met, exchanged lists, and made our requests known to the other side. We also went out in the field together to verify information. And at the next meeting, we would then acquaint the other side what it was that we found out and what could we offer in terms of bodies at specific locations for an exchange. Once an exchange was set up, meetings were held in different locations; but, in principle, it all went the same way. There would be a lull between the Serb and Federation lines, we would always come up with a suitable location at which we could meet up. Next, the bodies were brought in, exchanged, and then taken to their respective sides. It didn't necessarily always take place after combat. When I arrived, there were some mortal remains dating back to 1992. Many bodies were still unknown, and we have to conduct our searches to have an actual exchange. As a matter of fact, even to date, it is unfinished process.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to turn your attention now to a different topic and I would like to you focus, if you would, on the year 1995 and specifically on July of 1995. Do you recall at some point that month a meeting being scheduled near Sarajevo in Kiseljak? And, if you do, would you please tell the Trial Chamber what you remember about that meeting.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was meeting involving the state commission which was scheduled to take place in Kiseljak on the 11th of July, 1995. I was informed some two days before the meeting that there was going to be one, and I got in touch with the president of the commission of the 1st Krajina Corps to travel there together, to car pool. So we went to Mount Jahorina on the 10th, spent the night there, and, on the 11th, arrived in Lukavica. That was our last defence line. UNHCR armoured vehicles arrived to the location, bringing representatives of the commissions of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, the East Bosnian Corps, the 1st Krajina Corps, and the state commission. We all got in and went to Kiseljak through Federation-held territory. We came as far as the Kobiljaca pass where we were stopped by members of the HVO. That area was populated by Croats, and there was a HVO unit that was stationed there. It was very hot, and we were approached by a representative of that unit, a policeman. He wanted to know who we were, and a person from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps spoke to him for a few minutes and said they knew each other, and he was familiar with the terrain. He told the UNHCR representatives to raise the lids on the armoured vehicles so that we could get some fresh air because it was too warm. There was no reply from Kiseljak regarding the meeting, and we were allowed to disembark. We got out of the vehicles. There were seven APCs in total. I think there were four ahead, then mine, and two in the back. In any case, we waited outside for some two hours. The APCs in front of us went further to Kiseljak. Those who brought us there wanted to go as well, but the representatives of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps Commission did not allow that. He wanted to know what we were going to do, and we were told that neither Zenica, nor Tuzla Commission representatives arrived in Kiseljak and that we were to go back. However, we were unable because we no longer had sufficient APCs. Lubura, that was his name, got into touch with his corps, and I suppose his superior contacted the Main Staff; that is to say, General Tolimir. We were told that Tolimir had said that Srebrenica had fallen and that the APCs were to be let go. It was done in that way, and we were there in a tight situation because we didn't know how to go back. We managed to go back to Ilidza and after a couple of hours there, we managed to find a four-by-four with old Sarajevo pre-war registration plates. Our route took us just below the lines of the Federation and we drove fast. All I can tell you is that we used forest roads, and instead of the 15 kilometres that we had to traverse, we actually made 168 kilometres to finally end up in Jahorina, where we had left our vehicles. Once we got there, it was already dark and we were told not to go any further and to spend the night there. We were also told that there was going to be a meeting the next day at Sarajevo airport. Again, there were problems, because we had cancelled our accommodation. But in the end, we were accommodated somehow and waited the next day's negotiations. Nothing became of it, though. There were only mutual accusations that were exchanged. Their state commission, that is to say, Amor Masovic asserted that they were in Kiseljak asking why we didn't come. Bulajic said that the information he had received was that they did not appear than we had to be -- had to have been told not to come. In any case, there was no hope for any further constructive dialogue and the only thing was -- that was arranged was to have another meeting, nothing else. We left on the 12th, including the commission president and another member from the 1st Krajina Corps and myself from the Eastern Bosnia Corps. We got as far as Vlasenica, where we were held at a check-point. They told us we couldn't go any further because there was combat further afield. I was persistent. I explained why I had to continue, and eventually they let us through, up to Milici. At Milici there was a mixed check-point manned by our military police and the civilian police, and they did not allow us to go any further afield. At that location we could even hear infantry fire, and I asked whether there was anyone who could approve my departure and I was told that I should go to the Milici Brigade commander. I went to see him, introduced myself and asked him to let us through because the families of those missing had awaited me to see whether any agreement was reached on the prisoners. He said that we can go at our own risk, and I agreed to that. I told him we would try to get through. It was true that there was combat near the road and we heard infantry fire and mortar explosions, but we got through. I arrived Bijeljina and the relatives of those missing waited -- awaited me in front of the office. Although I was tired, I explained to them what the situation was, and I told them that I believed an exchange would be made possible which was something we couldn't have done before because we had nothing to offer. The Muslim side asked -- or conditioned a one-for-one exchange, and that is why we had nothing in particular to offer. That is also the reason why there were many exchanges which did not occur immediately after combat. And this pre-condition of theirs was a standing one. The next day, the chief of security told me that he had spoken to General Tolimir, who told him that he was to secure another hangar, another hall to receive prisoners. The figure that was specified was around 1300. I don't know whether the line of command and control was used by General Mladic or by the Chief of Staff to order the commander of the Eastern Bosnian Corps to convey to the head of the collection centre to carry out those preparations. Irrespective of that, those preparations were carried out, and two or three days later, the commander of the collection centre inquired why there were no prisoners coming and informed them that they had completed their part of the job. Since I didn't go to Batkovici in the course of those few days, and I didn't go to the corps either, I called the president of the Drina Corps Commission. His name was Slavko, I forgot his last name, but he was an elderly man. Since we used an open line, I asked him about it, and he told me that I had to do something or there would be nothing out of what had been agreed. It was put in a very -- in a way that wouldn't be understood by the other side. The next day, the chief of security informed me that a group of 20 wounded men from Srebrenica had arrived. I told him there was nothing I could do with 20 wounded people, because we had 101 prisoners, and he said that -- that most likely, something would take place later on. I didn't mention to him what the commission president had told me. The municipal president from Ugljevik arrived, accompanied by members of their commission for those who were captured or gone missing. They came to see me and I acquainted them with the situation. Then the municipal president offered for their units, that is to say, the 1st Majevica Unit which was in the process of being formed, as well as a reconnaissance unit of theirs to go to the area of combat, because there was still stranded groups there. His idea was basically to capture some more people, in order to have sufficient numbers of them for an exchange. I told him that it was neither up to his brigade commander, nor him, and that he was to go and see the corps commander. The representatives then went to see the corps commander, and they explained their request to him. General Simic refused, and he said that he was going to send some policemen to come up with a sufficient number of captured soldiers for an exchange. I never learned whether he did so; but, in any case, save for the 20, or in addition to the 20, there was another group totalling 168, I believe. After that, the situation was completely different, and we were ready to negotiate. A commission member from Brcko was in touch with the Tuzla Canton Commission, and in my previous testimony I said that I did not want to be in touch with them, because there were those who always expressed their doubts, saying, See, he has his own arrangement with the other side. And I know what such rumours mean, because I had spent a number of years in the security service. In any case, the contact was established through him and a meeting was arranged, at which I acquainted them with the situation. They wanted to see our lists. After the other group arrived, the ICRC visited them. I must tell you that I was somewhat upset at that moment, and I was toying with the idea of refusing them a visit because when a part of our brigade's territory was lost to the other side, for over 30 days the Tuzla authorities did not allow the ICRC to visit our captured personnel. I thought about it twice, and given the fact that we were on good terms with the ICRC and it was not their fault, I agreed to their visit. The chief consented to that, and we allowed them toe go in. There was also a simple explanation for it which was that the sooner they made their own lists, the sooner the situation would be clearer and exchanges would take place. Once they were there, they were also assisted medically. Between the contacts with this Tuzla Commission and our first exchange in September, there were about ten different meetings in different locations, such as in Brcko, or Lopare, trying to come up with the -- a procedural way to conduct that exchange, and they put a proposal that we would have an exchange, all for all, which was quite a turn from their one-for-one exchange position before. This was favourable because the 1st Krajina Corps did not have a sufficient numbers of prisoners. In the end, there was a group of 66 captured at Majevica and Lisace, plus another six. We got this personnel back and exchanged our 78 prisoners. Not all of them were fighters though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were some people who had been there earlier --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, may I interrupt you for a moment. This is the longest answer we ever have received in this trial. You have a lot to tell, but, in fact, Mr. Thayer was asking you about a specific event which was scheduled for the 11th. It is better for us and, for our understanding, if that could be an exchange of views and giving answers to specific questions by Mr. Thayer. And I think there are some topics I would like, and perhaps others would like to put a question as well to that. I would invite you to shorten your answers a bit so that we can follow in a better way.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may, because Mr. Mitrovic is a viva voce witness, the Trial Chamber doesn't have the benefit, necessarily, of his prior testimony and having the opportunity to read it as Your Honours do with the 92 ter testimony. Obviously I refrained from interrupting Mr. Mitrovic in his answer to my one specific question. The primary reason being that in the course of his narrative answer, he has very thoroughly, and I think clearly, touched on all the topics for which he has been called to testify, and I obviously do intend to follow up with some additional questions, go back. But Mr. Mitrovic's answers have been very much to the point of his testimony. I understand it was a long answer, but have no fear, Your Honours, we will go back and we will fill in those gaps and I think you'll understand the various subchapters to his testimony, as I clarify those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There's no doubt that all this information we received by the witness relates to this case, no doubt. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there seems to be a technical problem because of the speed at which the witness speaks. Line 8 -- page 8, line 19, there seems to -- a part of the sentence in missing which is actually when Lisace fell.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At Majevica. It's an area of defence of the 1st Majevica Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer will deal with that, I'm sure. May I -- as we have interrupted the witness, I just want to have an answer to two questions with which I want to clarify something. At one point you said: "We didn't have anything to offer ..." And I would like to get an explanation. What do you mean by that: "We didn't have anything to offer ..."?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did not have fighters from the Tuzla Corps whom we had taken prisoner. Those we had were from other areas, and from earlier, from the beginning of combat operations, for whom they were not too much interested in the places where they had come from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this clarification. My second clarification I would like to ask you for is, in relation to page 7, line 11. You said: "The next day, the chief of security informed me that a group of 20 wounded men from Srebrenica had arrived." Who was this chief of security? Which security unit are you referring to and who -- which is the name of this person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was the chief of the Department of Security of the Eastern Bosnia Corps, Milenko Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Excuse me, for the interruption.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Not at all. I think we all were sharing the same sentiments and I do have a number of follow-up questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, let's go back and talk about, just a moment, the meeting that you had scheduled, that had a been scheduled for the 11th of July in Kiseljak. At that time, in July of 1995, from your corps' area of responsibility, how many Serb soldiers from the Eastern Bosnian Corps were being held by the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 101 in Tuzla. These were soldiers from the Serbian units of the Eastern Bosnia Corps. However, there were others in Zenica, in Mostar, in other areas. From our corps, the prisoners were held in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Trial Chamber, out of those 101 Serb prisoners being held by the Muslims, where had they been captured; and approximately when?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One group was captured in January. I think it was January 1994. That was on the Majevica front. I think that the specific place was Jesenica. Another group was captured in March of the same year, I think, and they were captured at Siroki Njive. That is also on Majevica. Both places were held by the 1st Semberija Brigade, and these men were the soldiers of this brigade. However, before them, a part of the line of the 1st Majevica Brigade fell also on Majevica in the Lisace sector. That unit was detached, which was defending Lisace. Whether it was justified or not, that's another issue. But in any case, 61 soldiers survived. I think that 11 had been killed before Lisace fell. The fighting lasted for about three or four days. We tried to supply them with food, but they were left without food and water and eventually they surrendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember the exact dates, but it's possible that it was a little while before January 1994. It was certainly in winter when Lisace fell. There were also individuals, too. For example, a soldier may have strayed to the other side, or another one was revolted and then walked out into a minefield. And, in any case, the total number of our soldiers were 101; those who were held at the Tuzla prison. At that time, there were only, if you allow me, there were only five recently captured Muslim fighters. It was a sabotage unit that had infiltrated in our territory several days earlier, and they were the only ones that they were interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, a little later on in your answer of a few minutes ago, you referred to 66 from Lisace. What we have here in the transcript is 61 from Lisace. Can you tell us, do you remember whether it was 61 or 66 Serb prisoners who were captured at Lisace and being held in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I need to clarify that. 61 were captured at Lisace. One who was sick, very much so, was given to us as a present by Tuzla, because he was in a such bad state that he was supposed to die. And there were six others who had strayed or somehow happened to cross over to the other side. They were individuals. So there were those from Lisace, plus six others.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. That clarifies that. Thank you, Mr. Mitrovic. You've spoken a little bit already about the parents and relatives of these Serb soldiers being held in the Muslim prisons, being anxious to await your return from this meeting on 11 July. Can you tell the Trial Chamber whether these parents were organised at all around this issue of returning their sons to them?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were organised. A committee was formed in the territory of the Ugljevik municipality. It was elected by parents. They had a chairman. They came to see me, and when we started talking about soldiers from the territory of this municipality, I took the representative of those who were captured to the negotiations. I introduced him to the other side so that he could hear what the problems were and that he could truthfully relay the problems that exactly existed. Likewise from the area of the Bijeljina municipality, there was also a committee. The relatives elected their representatives and they also communicated with me. In addition to that, there were continuously individual whose sidesteps [as interpreted] official organs or representatives. They would come to see me in the territory of Ugljevik. After a certain number of contacts, the parents would get together. I would come there to inform them in detail about the meetings I had attended, what was agreed, and what the problems were.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you told us that this scheduled meeting from the 11th that did not happen actually then took place the next day on the 12th of July. And you told us how, after the meeting, you tried to return to Bijeljina but were stopped first at Vlasenica and at a check-point in Milici. You told us in your answer that you personally appealed to the brigade commander to let you pass, and it's just a technical matter, but I don't think the transcript reflected which brigade commander you had this contact with - can you just clarify that for the record, please - on the 12th of July, as you were held up in Milici.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I addressed the commander of the Milici Brigade. That was what the brigade was called. I don't know what his name was because I had never met him before and to this day, I don't know what his name was. And he was the one who allowed us to pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you then told us the very next day, the 13th of July, your corps security chief, Colonel Todorovic, told you that General Tolimir had told him to expect about 1300 prisoners. My first question is: Do you recall roughly how many Muslim prisoners, at that point, on the 13th of July, were at the Batkovic collection centre?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were between 40 and 50. I don't know the exact number. They were in one hangar in Batkovic. But the emphasises was not on the numbers, but, rather, that another hangar can -- should be made available so that such a big number of prisoners could be received because this hangar could receive only -- could receive up to 800 or even more people and it only had 40 to 60. So, if need be, it could accommodate much more people.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And putting aside, sir, for the moment, the issue of logistics of preparing Batkovic for receiving that many prisoners, what did this news mean to you in your role as president of the Eastern Bosnia Corps Exchange Commission; and what did it mean for the parents, the brothers and sisters of those Serb prisoners that we've been talking about?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We awaited impatiently this arrival. I was aware that I was resolving a problem that was difficult to resolve, and that is the exchange of prisoners of war. I also know that the 1st Krajina Corps would be able, this time, to achieve exchange, both with Tuzla and Zenica. Therefore, the parents and myself, as the president of the commission, and other members of the commission, worked on this. That was the goal of our work, to save those we could, to exchange those who were alive, to exchange the bodies of those who had been killed. So that it was a great relief to be able to count on the POWs that we would be able to exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You further told us that, I believe, two to three days passed, and when the prisoners didn't arrive, had you a conversation with a Drina Corps officer whose first name you remember was Slavko. And he urged you to try to get something done or -- I think you said something to the effect of "or nothing would happen." Can you tell the Trial Chamber, because I think that you said that this was stated in some kind of code so that the other side couldn't understand, what did you take this statement by this Slavko from the Drina Corps to mean?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an open-line. It wasn't military line, but a city line, and it was not to be expected that he would tell me that on such a line. It was sufficient for me to receive this warning, to see what I needed to do in order to get a number of POWs, not necessarily as many as I needed, but the more the better. That was always the principle. For me, the goal was for them to be allowed to leave and for those others to leave as well, because the war was at an end. That was what it meant. It meant I did not expect why he didn't tell me, but I could discern that something bad was happening and for the following reason: Because the relations in the area were very strained because earlier on, from the territory of the protected enclave of Srebrenica, the forces of Naser Oric infiltrated and committed a series of crimes and torched a series of villages in this area. Therefore, I was thinking along the following lines: What are these people who remained without their houses, without their families? They must be ready to do all kinds of bad things. But I did not expect that at any point what did happened would happen, but I thought that something bad might happen. And then as time went by, it turned out that many bad things did happen, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I want to show you a number of documents and ask you some questions about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note that the first document I would like to show Mr. Mitrovic was not included on our 65 ter list of exhibits. It's a document that we came across in preparing for Mr. Mitrovic's testimony. It is part of the Drina Corps collection that you've heard a lot about. We notified the Defence of it on our 65 ter list. I haven't had a chance to consult with the Defence as to their position on this document, but it is something that has, again, as I mentioned, been disclosed as part of the Drina Corps collection, and I would like to use it with Mr. Mitrovic. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Would you please be so kind to indicate which document are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, it's 65 ter 7423. And if there is no objection, I would move to add it to the 65 ter list of exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is from the government of the Republika Srpska State Commission for the Exchange of Prisoners of War and information memo. Mr. Tolimir, do you have any objection to add this document to the 65 ter exhibit list?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have no objections. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Since there is no objection, leave is granted to add it to the 65 ter exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And may we show 7423, please, to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, do you see a document on your screen? It may be rather hard to read. I have the original here. I'm not sure if it is going to be much easier to read. But with the Court Officer's assistance, I can give it to you so you at least have a choice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes. It should be given to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we scroll down in the original. Oh, I'm sorry, we can see it there in the original as it is. And if we go to the -- sorry. If you just return it to the state it was. I missed what I was looking for. It was right there in front of us. Thank you. And if we go to page 2 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, please take your time and read the document to yourself. We can see at the bottom that it's dated the 7th of July, 1995. And it is type-signed by Captain First Class Dragan Bulajic on behalf of the State Commission for Exchange of Prisoners of War.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could go back to the first page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, when you've acquainted yourself with the document, please just let us know and I'll continue your examination.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have read it, so please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, again, we can see that this is a document sent from the RS, the Republika Srpska, State Commission for Exchange of POWs, type-signed by Mr. Bulajic. And the subject is a -- is: "Meeting with Muslim and Croatian," and it is garbled in our version, and it refers to a meeting planned for the 11th of July, 1995, in Kiseljak. And we can see that it's been sent to the POW Exchange Commissions for a number of corps, including the Eastern Bosnia Corps. My question to you, sir, is simply: How does this document correspond or not correspond to the meeting on the 11th of July that you told us about earlier in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the meeting as mentioned in the dispatch, the one scheduled for the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution would tender 65 ter 7423.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell me -- no, thank you. I got it. Thank you. It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter document 7423 shall be assigned Exhibit P2271. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I take the opportunity to mention that the Registry will circulate a memo with the correction of the wrong number given to one document. This problem was raised by Mr. Gajic at the beginning of today's hearing. The document will be P2270 instead of the previous number. But it will be -- will contain -- will be contained in the memorandum.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: With your leave, Your Honour, just to mention that Exhibit P2270 shall be assigned to the 65 ter document 2240. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic, let's look at another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we may have 65 ter 3978 on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I think you'll find this a little bit more legible than the last. But if you'd like the original, I have it here. So please just let us know if you need to look at the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could scroll down in the B/C/S, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, when you're done reading the first page - and please take your time - just let us know when you're ready to go to the second page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can we scroll down in the English, please, just to catch the bottom of the document in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, again, whenever you're ready, sir.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read it. Go ahead. I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. If we could back to the first page in both the B/C/S and the English. What we have here, for the record, is a telegram type-signed by General Tolimir. And it's the 20th of January, 1995. And the heading is: "Prisoner exchange, authorisation." We can see that in the first line General Tolimir writes that we authorise the POW commissions from the Drina Corps and the Eastern Bosnian Corps to establish contact with the Muslim Corps, prisoner exchange representatives. And in the second paragraph, General Tolimir refers to some VRS soldiers who were captured at Lisace. Are those the same Lisace prisoners about whom you spoke about earlier, Mr. Mitrovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I won't read into the record at length from the telegram. But General Tolimir says that: "The Eastern Bosnia Corps Commission will prepare and offer a list of Muslims that we plan to exchange for the Lisace prisoners." And he says that: "The number of prisoners on the list must not exceed the number of persons they are asking for, including the persons being asked for by the Eastern Bosnia Corps Commission." If we go to the second page in English, General Tolimir specifically says in this telegram: "During the negotiations, do not show any interest in Lisace prisoners. On the contrary. In an opportune moment, misinform them that Lisace fighters are not an exchange priority." And then in the following paragraph he says that: "By means of misinformation, we intend to make the Muslims attach little significance to the Lisace prisoners, thus ensuring their swift and favourable exchange." Sir, putting the merits and substance of General Tolimir's words here to the side, can you tell the Trial Chamber, in your experience, what role did the VRS Main Staff and General Tolimir and the intelligence and security sector, or the -- or the security administration play in organising, arranging, and executing these prisoner exchanges?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their role, for the most part, was to give or deny their approval. The commissions actually initiated proposals. As I said yesterday, I was under an obligation, for example, to prepare a list of what we want from the other side and what we have to offer. We then had to acquaint the corps commander and, upon this -- upon his approval, we were to dispatch that information to the security administration of the Main Staff for their approval. They never failed to approve it, and occasionally they also provided us with some suggestions. If what we sent was unclear, they requested clarification. I mentioned that yesterday. We always had several different drafts that we could table during a meeting so that we would secure at least some kind of exchange, if not in totality, then at least partially. There were also some instructions such as co-ordinating the work of the commission in a general area, and that was their role. Without all the approvals as specified, the commission president and the Commission for Exchange, as a whole, could not negotiate. That was the route. First, the chief of security had to be informed when I was president, and before, it was all the commander who was informed directly, and then he informed the Main Staff by way of dispatch. The state commission was also informed. The previous president sent his proposals to the state commission, but I stopped that practice, and they would be informed from the Main Staff. That's what Bulajic told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, this telegram that we're looking at, is this the type of communication that you would receive from the Main Staff during the course of your duties; or is this unusual in any way?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say the following: What we can see on this piece of paper does not necessarily reflect what went on in the field. We had no need to overestimate or underestimate the importance of the Lisace people. They were well aware what they had. It was a painful spot, because the most people, up to that point, were killed at that operation. I simply said that I wanted the people from Lisace. I did not try to place too little or too much stress on the importance of those prisoners for us. We can see from all this -- for example, this Causevic person, or the brothers, it seems that there is a mention of them being in Vlasenica. I'm not sure. In any case, the East Bosnia Corps Commission could not implement any exchange for the needs of the Drina Corps. The relationship was so poor that when the Tuzla Commission met with the Drina Corps Commission, and most of their commission were people from Zvornik, such meetings lasted less than five minutes. They would start arguing immediately and go their own ways. There were never any results. However, when we set up a meeting, the Drina Corps representatives would arrive. And it always ended up in arguments and fights, and it was impossible for us to do anything because they were on such bad terms. We couldn't negotiate for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution would tender 65 ter 3978.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 3978 shall be assigned Exhibit P2272. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's look at another document. This is 65 ter 5688, and I'm afraid this one may also be a little bit light on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So I do have the original for you, sir, to look at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: With the assistance of the Court Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: With the assistance of the Court Officer. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, are you able to read this document from the record? Or would you prefer to receive a hard copy as well?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I see your assistant is assisting you with a hard copy. Thank you for that, Mr. Gajic. If we could go to the second page in English, and stay with the B/C/S where we are, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think we -- there was a little bit missing on the bottom of the first page. I don't know if you were able to pick it up on your version or not. I know when I was looking at e-court, it hadn't displayed the entire document in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just now the entire document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Oh, indeed, it did catch it, Mr. President. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we should go to the second page. Thank you. Mr. Thayer, you should switch off your microphone when you have an internal discussion with your colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, there is a third page to the document, if the Chamber has had an opportunity to review this second page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And we are now on the second page in B/C/S as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I see you've had an opportunity to review this document. And we can see on this last page that it was authored by Colonel Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could back to the first page of the document, please. For the record, it's a telegram from Colonel Beara, dated the 11th of May, 1995. And it's addressed to various corps security departments, as well as to the POW Exchange Commissions of various corps, including the Eastern Bosnia Corps. And we can see in the first paragraph of Colonel Beara's telegram that he refers to a meeting of the State Commission for POW Exchange which was attended by various representatives of the corps commissions, with the Muslim Commission, held at the airport in Sarajevo on 5 May 1995. And if we can just go to the second page in English. Stay on this page in the original. He refers to VRS soldiers being held at Vijenac.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber whether you know anything about the prisoners who were detained in or at Vijenac? Which VRS corps were those prisoners a member of, where Vijenac is, in which corps, if you know? And if you don't know anything about what he is referring to when he refers to Vijenac prisoners, please say so as well and I will move on.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think those were the Serb soldiers captured at Vijenac, which is at Mounted Ozren. They were from the 1st Krajina Corps. They weren't held there. It was in the area of responsibility of the Tuzla Corps. Vijenac is the name of the positions those soldiers had been at when they were captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And so that would be in the same way that you referred to the Lisace prisoners who were captured at Lisace as the Lisace prisoners. The -- Colonel Beara is referring to the Vijenac prisoners as those prisoners who were captured at the Vijenac location. Is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. He refers to a meeting at the Sarajevo airport on 5 May 1995. And do you recall whether you attended that meeting? I know you attended a lot of them, but does this particular meeting ring any bells for you? And, if not, again, I'll move on with my questions, if you have no specific recollection of this meeting.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Save for the meeting in June, I attended two meetings at the airport. I don't know whether this may have been the first or the second. I think it was the first. We discussed all the issues we had in the presence of the president and representatives of the state commissions and the commissions of the corps. If this is indeed the meeting have I in mind, nothing was agreed at it. It lasted for three or four hours, and nothing became of it, in terms of exchanges. Following which, Bulajic and Masovic had their own private conversation discussing which groups to exchange. First they had these arguments at the table and then they talked to each other. Nothing was achieved, and another meeting was held. Perhaps you have a dispatch referring to it. When we analysed things in detail, including the previous exchanges, meetings were -- minutes were held --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Minutes were kept.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I asked to see everything that was done as part of the various exchanges, such as the East Bosnia Corps Commission. During such exchanges, there was no participation of the state commissions, and I refused to sign it. Their member refused to sign it as well, and we wanted to have a clear distinction between who did what. Whenever the state commission took part, it had to be clearly stipulated as opposed to any other exchanges. All these matters were canvassed at the second meeting. We carried out a detailed analysis and when Masovic offered to me -- well, he asked me, Does this name mean anything to you? And I told him, I think it is a fighter of mine. And then he said, Well, let's have him exchanged. I asked him, How? And then he said, Well, I'll see to it with Bulajic. He will give us something and we'll give him to you. It couldn't be. We had to have an approval of all the institutions and families, otherwise it is a dirty game. In the end, that person was exchanged, but it cost the families 28.000 German marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just ask you one further question before we break for our first break.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could go to page 3 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And this will be the second page of the original. The last page in -- in your version, Mr. Mitrovic. Colonel Beara refers here, if we look at the second-to-the last paragraph, he says: "The Eastern Bosnia Corps Commission for POW exchange should work on creating conditions for the exchange of detainees from Stolice and Lisace, in combination with a number of civilians the Muslims are asking for and whom we have put on trial." The reference here to Stolice, can you tell the Trial Chamber what Colonel Beara is referring to? Detainees from Stolice.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's probably the group I mentioned that had been captured at Duge Njive. It was another area like Lisace, except that this one was called Stolice. And there was this third location, Jablanica, I think. These are all locations or positions held by the Serb forces when they were captured by the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And is that in the area of Mount Majevica, sir?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's all at Mount Majevica, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And so would these prisoners be among the 101 that you referred to earlier in the your testimony?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution would tender 65 ter 5688.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter document 5688 shall be assigned Exhibit P2273. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note we're a minute beyond the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, we must have our first break of this afternoon now, and we will resume quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer. Please continue. And bear in mind the time you have spent with this witness, around two and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think I should come in at or under our estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I see the transcript is not working, at least in e-court. I don't see anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, you have the same problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I've got the same problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's stopped with the words recess taken at 3.00, nothing more is recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, is your system working?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's working now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: So with the help and the assistance of the Registrar, we managed to get back into the transcript. We had problems with the three screens of the Judges. And I heard from Mr. Gajic everything is working now. Mr. Thayer, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. May we see 65 ter 4025, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, we have a one-page telegram here dated 4th of June, 1995. I again have the original, if it is easier for you to read. Please let us know if what's on your screen isn't legible enough for you. We can furnish you with the original.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's better in hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, with the assistance of the Court Usher, a hard copy should be given to the witness. Mr. Tolimir, can you read it on the screen, the B/C/S version? You are nodding. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, when you've had an opportunity to review this telegram, please let us know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It's two pages in the English, so we'll need to go to page 2 in a couple moments in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I see you've had a chance to read it. For the record, again, it's a telegram, and it's type-signed from General Tolimir, dated the 4th of June, 1995. It's addressed to the, among other entities, the commissions for POW exchanges, including your commission, the Eastern Bosnia Corps Exchange Commission. And in it, General Tolimir writes that the commander of the VRS Main Staff and his staff maintain the positions presented in this telegram, and that: "We believe it is necessary to insist on observing the all-for-all principle." Can you tell the Trial Chamber, if you recall, Mr. Mitrovic, what this telegram is about? What is General Tolimir referring to here?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The dispatch talks about the need to insist in the negotiations on the all-for-all principle. That means that we should release all imprisoned persons from all Serbian prisons in exchange for everyone who is imprisoned in Muslim prisons; that is to say, prisons of the Federation army. That never happened. It could not happen because everyone had its own problems. Each corps had its problems. Some had prisoners, others didn't, or they had a few. So that never until the expiry of my mandate, the all-for-all exchange never happened at the level of the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. We'll take a little bit more about some of those issues in a little while.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution will tender 65 ter 4025.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter 4025 shall be assigned Exhibit P2274. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we have 65 -- I beg your pardon. P02250, please. I'm handing the original to the Court Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And she may give it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, this is the last telegram I'll be showing you during my examination-in-chief. It's -- I know it is two solid pages. Please take your time and acquaint yourself with the contents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, it seems to be a lengthy document. Perhaps you can point out for the witness, and for the others present here, to which part you specifically will refer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I can do that, Mr. President. I'll just take him through the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, let's move through the document together. We can see, for the record, that it is a telegram emanating from the Main Staff of the VRS intelligence and security sector, and its date is 3 September 1995. And it's addressed to the commanders and intelligence and security departments of several corps, including your corps, the Eastern Bosnia Corps. The heading is: "Exchange of prisoners, report." We can see in the first paragraph that General Tolimir, who authored this telegram, we can see at the last page, it's his typed signature. In the first paragraph, General Tolimir writes about the commanders of the 1st Krajina Corps and Eastern Bosnia Corps contacting the commander of the General Staff - that would be General Mladic - and informed him of the protests of the families of VRS members captured at Vijenac and Lisace and their requests to make it a priority to exchange the persons captured at these two localities. And in this telegram, General Tolimir describes what the Eastern Bosnia Corps commander - I think we'll all agree that would be General Novica Simic - told General Mladic that the families of the Lisace prisoners were demanding that only those prisoners be exchanged for the captured Muslims at Batkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we go to the next page in English, the top of the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And this is still on the first page of your version, sir. General Tolimir writes: "In addition, the families of the persons captured from Vijenac want the exchange to proceed on the basis of the all-for-all principle and to release around 150 captured Muslims from the Batkovic collection centre for the captured VRS soldiers from Lisace." Now, let's jump down a couple of paragraphs. General Tolimir writes: "In addition, through the state commission for the exchange of prisoners of war, the VRS Main Staff insisted on an all-for-all exchange, since the number of captured Muslims in our prison [sic] is smaller than the number of captured VRS members in Muslim prisons." And, sir, just to make sure we're literally on the same page, it's the first page of your document, the third paragraph. Do you see where I'm reading from, Mr. Mitrovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I have read it already.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. General Tolimir continues: "However, the Muslim side is blocking all exchanges on the basis of both principles, making it conditional that a larger number of Muslims from the area of Srebrenica and Zepa be exchanged than the number of Muslims we have in our prisons." Now, we just saw that June document, that 4 June document from General Tolimir to the various corps POW commissions, telling you to observe the all-for-all principle. And here we see that the Main Staff is insisting on an all-for-all exchange here. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what General Tolimir is referring to here, particularly when he is referring to: "... the Muslim side blocking all exchanges on the basis of both principles, making it conditional that a larger number of Muslims from the area of Srebrenica and Zepa be exchanged than the number of Muslims we have in our prisons"? Can you explain that a little bit, please, to the Trial Chamber, what your understanding of this is?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the very beginning of combat operations, an agreement was reached in Geneva, I think, between the Serbian and the Muslim side. I think that Radovan Karadzic, the president, attended this meeting, and so did Alija Izetbegovic and Tudjman. As far as I remember, it was then agreed to carry out an all-for-all exchange with the exception of those who had been criminally prosecuted. The exchange did not occur because there was a deception about it. All Serbs who were imprisoned by Croats and Muslims were criminally prosecuted and the Serbs did not criminally prosecute the Muslims and the Croats, so they were supposed to release everyone and not to receive anyone. That was why the all-for-all exchange never really occurred; whichever side insisted on it. We were the side that more often insisted, but, at the state level, it never happened. Sometimes corps would carry out exchanges through negotiations with the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's -- excuse me. Let's look at a couple of other paragraphs, and we'll follow up on that a little bit, Mr. Mitrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could go to page 3 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And this is the last paragraph on your first page, sir. General Tolimir writes that, "The corps commissions" -- again, it's the bottom paragraph on the first page of your original: "The corps commissions are not objectively informing the families of the captured soldiers and trying to individually arrange exchanges with the Muslim side, which is not reciprocal, and it is to our detriment in circumstances where we have a smaller number of prisoners. This is particularly indicative when this is also requested by the corps commands who know all the relevant facts, particularly when the principle every command should strive for has not been observed, to capture as many enemy soldiers as is the number of our members captured by the enemy." Let me draw your attention to one final paragraph and then I'll put my question to you, Mr. Mitrovic. If we turn to page 2 of your original version, and I'm referring to the third paragraph in your version. This is page 4 of the English, please. If we look at the second paragraph in English, and again, this is the third paragraph in your version. General Tolimir writes: "The exchange commission chairmen must view the exchange proposal integrally, as does the Main Staff of the VRS, since, so far, the Main Staff has made the necessary number of prisoners available for the corps commissions in circumstances where they did not have a sufficient number of captured enemy soldiers to exchange for all the captured members of their corps. Security organs and exchange commission chairmen must also avoid using parents' bitterness because it is not possible to exchange prisoners who have been in prison for quite some time, particularly because the Main Staff of the VRS is not responsible for this situation; rather, it is the result of the small number of enemy soldiers captured by our units." Were you able to follow that paragraph in your version, sir, that I just read? Okay.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, can you give the Trial Chamber an approximate number, if you can remember, of how many Serb soldiers, throughout -- or from the various VRS corps were being held by the opposing side in July of 1995? Can you give us a rough number of how many Serb prisoners of war there were? Not just from your corps, but if you can recall approximately from the other corps.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never knew that, so I cannot recall, because I never had a chance on any basis to receive the number of prisoners who had been taken from any of the other corps. I only know the number of those who had been captured and who were soldiers of our Eastern Bosnia Corps. At the meetings of the state commission, a total number was never mentioned, so I couldn't remember what the total number was. That was never provided, and I was not aware of the total number.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, General Tolimir writes here in this -- on page 4 in that paragraph that: "The VRS Main Staff has made the necessary number of prisoners available for the corps commissions in circumstances where they did not have a sufficient number of captured enemy soldiers to exchange for all the captured members of their corps."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is page 4 of --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Of the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- the English?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, again, this is page 2 of the B/C/S. Yes, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, just for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Was that your understanding of the situation at this time, in September of 1995, sir?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Previously, when I was not the commission president, because a dispatch was shown to me last time I was here, some kind of caution on the conduct of the corps. It seems that from Batkovic they were taking people to be exchanged, whoever they wanted to. Later on, however, they had no one to take, so the people who had been left, some 50 of them at Batkovic, were not of any interest to the other side. And there was no hindrance for any corps to take them for an exchange. There's a mention made of civilian exchanges. It all was supposed to bear fruit, at least on our side, but it was probably the Federation authorities who prevented it. The Tuzla canton commission had a framework arrangement with us, and there were some able-bodied men in -- who were Muslim in Bijeljina. I provided them with such figures, expecting that there would be an exchange. However, it was not possible. In the dispatch it was also mentioned that there should be a one-for-one exchange which was unrealistic because these people were able bodied but they were not POWs.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, again, in this paragraph, General Tolimir tells the security organs and exchange commission chairmen that they must avoid using the parents' bitterness. And when he says that "the VRS Main Staff is not responsible for this situation," and that it is "...rather, the result of the small number of enemy soldiers captured by our units," how does that square with your understanding of the situation in September of 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This probably refers to the previous period, not only the situation as was in September. The municipal president and members of the committee visited General Tolimir, asking for help. They also asked for help from the state commission and were told to go to see Karadzic because the VRS did not have sufficient numbers of prisoners to make them available to us. Nobody wanted to see the parents dissatisfied. We had to swallow many a thing that others may not necessarily be aware of. The army placed people in different facilities, and those interested usually came to see me. If they wanted to see somebody from the army, the general would usually send me when they went to see the municipal president in Bijeljina in order to explain why such an exchange could not occur. There is another thing that the general may not be aware of. When, upon our insistence [Realtime transcript read in error "assistance"], they were transferred to Batkovic, then the 1st Krajina Corps asked for everyone to be transferred to Banja Luka or to Kotorsko, near Doboj to the prison there, so that they could have a comprehensive exchange. The commander of the 1st Krajina Corps did not want to give up from that request, and I prepared the parents for that. I arranged that the road to Batkovic should be blocked should buses arrive to take those captured to Banja Luka. I arranged that tractors be placed on the road. I was fully ready to go ahead with that and I don't think anybody would have approved of that, at least not in formal terms. But no one contradicted it either. The 1st Krajina Corps Commission did not get involved to have those prisoners exchanged, and there was an opportunity to secure sufficient numbers of prisoners in this period of time for an exchange. It did not occur, however, but we did provide some 40 prisoners from the area of Srebrenica, and they left.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Page 39, line 5, upon our insistence.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And by this time, in early September - this document is dated the 3rd of September, 1995 - approximately how many Muslim prisoners actually arrived at the Batkovic camp, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think 168. That's what I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you've already told us to today that General Tolimir had told Colonel Todorovic to expect 1300 prisoners who never arrived to Batkovic. You said that you believed that bad things had happened to them. Did you ever learn, Mr. Mitrovic, that negotiations at a high level between the Serb and Muslim sides for the exchange of prisoners, in particular, the prisoners -- or, in particular, with respect to men from Zepa, failed, owing to the VRS's inability to account for the prisoners they had taken following the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to Zepa, we didn't receive any such prisoners. As for these negotiations at a state level, I'm not familiar with those.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, just a few more questions, sir. Again, referring to the 1300 prisoners who never arrived at Batkovic. The Trial Chamber has heard a lot of testimony about several thousand Muslim men and boys being executed in the Zvornik and Bratunac Brigades' area of responsibility and buried there, following the fall of Srebrenica. And you've already referred to these 1300 prisoners who never arrived, that you thought something bad had happened to. As president of the Eastern Bosnia Corps Exchange Commission, how would it have affected your job had the Muslim side and the ICRC found out the truth about what happened to those thousands of men and boys who had been taken prisoner and then later executed, following the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Concerning those who had been captured and executed, I didn't know about any of that at the time. I think that the Muslim side had their doubts, so we conducted our negotiations without specific problems because neither I nor the other side knew the truth. We tried to do what we could. I have to say, though, that when the first exchange occurred on the 29th of September of 1995, the president of the cantonal commission said, Thanks to you, these people are alive. I don't know where he gained that impression of his, but the exchange went ahead, in any case. The following exchange was going to be an all-for-all exchange, but we took everyone from Batkovic and, together with the 1st Krajina Corps, following the approval of the Main Staff, we took the people they had, in order to have an exchange of all those who were captured with those captured on the other side, specifically the Tuzla Cantonal Commission and the Zenica Commission. I think it happened on the 25th of December, after a round -- several rounds of talks. It was finally approved and agreed upon, and they were exchanged at the Sockovac river in Gracanica. Everyone was exchanged for everyone else. All those that the 1st Krajina Corps Commission sought arrived from Tuzla and Zenica. We also received all those we wanted to have. Having done that, there were no further demands, no more people to exchange, and the Batkovic centre was closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how would your job in July through December of 1995 have been affected, had the VRS had in its custody, let's just say, 7.000 living Muslim prisoners available to exchange?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have welcomed that. Anyone would who is familiar with what a war is and who knows what it is to lose one's dearest and nearest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it would be useful if Mr. Thayer provided a reference where this figure of 7.000 people who went missing comes from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, honestly, I think that number that I used of approximately 7.000 people which I believe is consistent with what we have in the indictment and what we have argued and established throughout the trial, thus far, is a fair one to put to the witness, and he has answered the question. I only have one or two more questions. And I believe I'm at my time and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please, we're talking about this objection by Mr. Tolimir at the moment. Mr. Tolimir, Mr. Thayer gave -- or put to the witness an approximation. He said: "... had the VRS had in its custody, let's just say, 7.000 living Muslim prisoners available to exchange?" He could have said 5.777 or any other figure. He received his -- the answer he was asking for, and now Mr. Thayer should go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And I will move quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I base my objection, or, rather, it was justified because Mr. Thayer referred to the indictment. But it wasn't proven. Therefore, these are assumptions, brush-stroke numbers, as you, yourself, specified. This is a trial. I beg him to be more precise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, no doubt, at the end of this trial, we will find out what could be seen as the truth. But, at this moment, it was just approximation. Please carry on, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, the document that we've been looking at, again, is dated 3rd of September, 1995. The Trial Chamber has heard testimony in this case that a day after issuing this telegram, where he's blaming the corps for not taking enough prisoners and telling the POW commissions not to let the parents' bitterness be a factor, the Trial Chamber heard evidence that General Tolimir's sector dispatched a security administration officer late in the night of 4 September, into the early morning hours of 5 September, to the Vanekov Mlin prison to take custody of Colonel Avdo Palic, the former commander of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina's Rogatica Brigade --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, to avoid an objection by Mr. Tolimir, I would kindly ask you to rephrase your question and not to put a leading question to the witness. Just ask him about his knowledge about the fate of this person. I think it is much more helpful for your case than to put -- to put evidence of another witness to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we see P02182. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, we can see here a document which is titled: "Receipt." And it states: "On the exclusion of the detainees on the 5th of September ... at 0100 hours for the needs of the ... intelligence sector of the VRS Main Staff ... Avdo Palic ... transferred ... following the order of Dragan Tomic." We can see the various stamps and signatories. Were you aware, Colonel, at any time between July and December of 1995, that a brigade colonel of the opposing forces, the brigade commander, had been transferred, essentially, in your backyard at this prison.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never in Vanekov Mlin, which is across the road from the barracks. I never knew of anyone being detained there. I didn't know that it used to be a detention unit for our own soldiers, when there was no room in the detention cell in the barracks. I was asked about this in the MUP as well. They asked me about it when they were looking for this prisoner and when the government of the RS was interested in finding out the truth. The first time I went there was in 1996, I think, when there were several civilians brought there. Together with the ICRC, we picked them up and took them to Brcko. We handed them over without any pre-conditions, although we were promised the bodies of some killed people for them. But this was all finished by that time. Let me say this as well. This is nothing to do with Batkovic. The command of the collection centre at Batkovic had no competence in this part. That is also probably why I was completely ignorant of this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, in your experience as a member of -- and president of this POW exchange commission, what did it mean, if anything, to you or to any side to have in its custody a prisoner of the stature of a brigade commander? What value, if any, did having such a prisoner have, in terms of potential exchanges?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it would have been of great importance. Since there were conditions put to most of the exchanges, this would have been a very important one to have a more favourable exchange. It would have been expected to receive far more soldiers for this person because he was an officer. Unless, of course, the other side also had captured officers, then officers would be exchanged for officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: My last question, sir: You've got security experience. You've served for many years on this exchange commission. You've had a lot of experience with exchanges. Do you know of any reason to divert thousands of prisoners of war from Batkovic and to house them in little schools and buildings around the Zvornik area?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no such people were transferred from Batkovic to different buildings in the area of the municipality of Zvornik, unless it happened in 1992. But when I arrived in the commission, such things did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: My --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, again, I wanted to ask for a reference, according to which some prisoners were transferred from Batkovic to a number of schools in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I can clarify that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: My question, in fact, and, again, I apologise for the confusing question. My question was, sir: Can you think of any reason why thousands of prisoners who were captured in the Bratunac Brigade and Zvornik Brigade areas of responsibility, instead of being brought up to Batkovic, were placed in schools and buildings scattered throughout the Zvornik Brigade area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who ordered it, and if anyone ordered such transfers, or if it was a move that was decided upon by the lower-ranking units. Given that my corps took no participation in it, and as the president of the commission, I was not familiar with those events, there's nothing to say. I didn't even know that they were transferred to Zvornik. I thought that there were a few places where people were captured close to the area of responsibility, but I am unaware of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And based on your experience, both as a security officer and as a member of the commission, can you think of any explanation why that would have been done, instead of sending those prisoners up to Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why it was done. In my view, it would have been good or justified to have them sent to Batkovic. From a dispatch, you could see that the Drina Corps objected as well, that their people were taken by the 1st Krajina Corps and the commission of the Eastern Bosnia Corps, and we had not captured those people. Now what their needs were is something I don't know. And then there was this order stating that we were to capture people if we wanted to exchange anyone, and then we simply told the Tuzla commission, We don't have enough people. We have to wait. And then there was this idea to have it combined with civilians, and, in the end, exchanges took place along different lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, you should come to an end. You promised to be shorter than three hours in your examination-in-chief and now you extended this time already.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, that concludes my examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mitrovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Thayer. Mr. Mitrovic, now the accused, Mr. Tolimir is conducting his cross-examination. Mr. Tolimir, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I greet everyone present. May there be peace to this house. I hope that this day of trial will be completed in accordance with God's will rather than as I wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to greet Mr. Mitrovic, and I wish him a pleasant stay among us. And I will also ask him to give brief answers to my questions so that I would have sufficient time to ask him all the questions I planned because we have already spent a lot of time. And also, please start answering the questions only when you see that the cursor on the transcript stops. I will also try to start asking questions only once you have finished providing your answer. Thank you. We'll start from the last questions. You were asked whether the sector sent someone to take over Avdo Palic. You were asked that on page 43, whether, on the 5th of September, a man was sent for this purpose. This is my question: Were you aware then or later, that is to say, did you learn from the detention centre warden, or anyone else at, perhaps, an exchange that you attended, whether this man came to Vanekov Mlin with a task to take him without leaving any trace, that he took him away, or did he bring a paper requesting that he be taken from there, or did he have the authority to take him away? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two years ago, when I was called to crime prevention service in the MUP, when they asked me about this, in connection with the information about Palic, I was surprised because, until that point, I had not heard the name nor of the man in the military circles. So that I did not know that he had ever stayed there, which one can hear in the media, that he has been found dead in the area of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
