utterances.text: Can you please speak a bit more slowly.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And be as brief as possible. Just answer my question. Something was shown to you here, a statement, a confirmation, about taking over Avdo Palic which was signed by guard Veselin Marijanovic. It was issued and certified by Milan Savic, as the warden, and it says that Pecanac took over Avdo Palic. Have you seen this certificate earlier; yes or no? We can see it on the screen again.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have seen the receipt, but I don't know any of the persons who signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And is it customary to take over a detainee from a guard or should it, rather, be one of the administrative or managerial organs, the prison warden or someone like that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was always necessary to have the approval of the corps, whether of the commander or the chief of security, which would be sent to the commander of the collection centre. On the basis of that, a detainee could be taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mitrovic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On page 45, line 10, the Prosecutor asked you whether you were aware of any reasons to remove 1.000 POWs from Batkovic to Zvornik, and then, later on, it was changed but it was not deleted from the record. So can you please tell us the following: Did you have information from the Muslims that they requested a certain number of persons from you, from Batkovic, persons whom they listed as missing, and did they ever specify the number of these persons who they were looking for, they or the ICRC? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was clear, at least during the time while I was in the commission, that some people were requested but these were those who had died and this referred to the exchange of dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But if a side was looking for someone, was it obliged to tell you directly or through the ICRC who were these persons that they were looking for from the other side? Were they obliged to submit a list to you? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably that was supposed to be the way, but we directly made requests to one another and we informed the ICRC, so they were aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When you worked on that directly, did you then ever directly receive from the Muslim Commission the information about the number of missing persons they were looking for, and did you ever receive a list of such persons? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean the events around Srebrenica, I never received any list. And as for the others, it was well-known who they were looking for, who we had, and what was requested.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D228 is the document we would need to show now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see where it says: "Republika Srpska, Ministry of Defence." It was submitted to the Ministry of Justice liaison office with ICTY --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It should not be broadcast because it's a confidential document. I repeat: It should not be broadcast. It's a confidential document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Then please do not broadcast it. Just let us see it on the screens so the witness can see it as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You can see that what they received was a memo about the number of persons who were handed over from Batkovici --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please turn to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: -- because the list of Muslims who were exchanged from the Batkovic collection centre was provided. You're probably familiar with this list, which has a total of 171 persons. Please explain, with regard to the first person, don't read the name, but it says that the date of arrival at the Batkovic collection centre is the 18th of June -- July 1995, and the date of departure is the 10th of July, 1995. Is it an error or --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's illogical, so it must be an error. Because, on the 10th of July, as far as I know, no one was brought to Batkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think we may be able to agree with the Defence. And this was gone into in the prior trial. Just for the Trial Chamber's information, that this date of 10 July 1995 is a transposition and it should actually be 7 October; instead of 10/7, it would be 7/10, and I -- I don't imagine we've got much dispute about that. If we do, then I stand corrected, but I think this was gone into before and I don't expect there is a dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, are you aware of that? We have seen this document before. I don't recall in detail. But if you -- most of the entries are from September or October, except the third one, with a date of 24th of July, 1995. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mitrovic. Is it possible that the person from number 1 was exchanged in October rather than in July, and that the day and the month have been transposed when noted here?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my estimate, it is only possible that the person was not exchanged at the time at all but, rather, transferred to Kotorsko near Doboj, and that the person was only exchanged on the 25th of December, the 24th or the 25th, when there was an all-for-all exchange. At least my commission did not have any exchanges on this date.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mitrovic. Please tell us, when did you exchange the soldiers from Lisace and others that Eastern Bosnia Corps was requesting? Can you tell us the date and time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 29th of September, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please review the list now, and just have a look at the dates of arrival to Batkovic and departure from it so you would be able to tell me which exchange is which when I ask you that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please also show page 2 to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You're probably familiar with this list, as it was made in co-operation with the detention authorities in Batkovic, and it was available to the commission.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please look at the following page after number 57. Thank you. And the next one, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So you have seen all the dates on which exchanges were carried out. The names are listed in alphabetical order.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can we please show the last page. The last page ends with number 171.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You can also see the note which says the said persons from the list were registered by the ICRC, and ICRC representatives were present when they were exchanged. This is my question for you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we please see the last page in English. Thank you. Now your question, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic, as ICRC representatives were present, were they able to see how many people were requested and how many were held in prisons because they visited prisons including the collection centre in Batkovic; yes or no? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The International Committee of the Red Cross had certain documents at its disposal. For example, they had a book of missing persons from Srebrenica. They gave me a copy. I raised certain objections because there were a number of persons with the same first and last names and all the other personal data, so it was obviously that it was one and the same person. I told them that it should be checked and then that some of them should be deleted because it was an obvious error in the book. So, that is to say, they did have the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you still have that book in your files or in the archives in the commands for which you worked?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. Because I handed over all the documents to Lieutenant-Colonel Miso Petricevic at the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you possibly remember the number of all Muslim POWs from Srebrenica in the book that was provided to you by the ICRC? Please make a pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was around 8.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did all the 8.000 people include also the wrong information, the double names and so on?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were they intentionally registered like that and was there a big number of such cases, or were there just a few that you noticed? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was quite a number of such entries. I don't know the exact number. I underlined them in the book. I showed it to them, and I indicated that there could be more but that I did not have sufficient time to go through it all in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you perhaps provide a copy of the book when you get back? Could you find it in the archives and provide it to the Defence while the proceedings are still going on? That is to say, as soon as possible. Do you think there is any possibility of that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no possibility because I wonder where the archives are. A unit of the Joint Command of Bosnia and Herzegovina is stationed there now, so that it is inaccessible. One could see how many copies the ICRC have. I don't know. I can check with the ICRC in Bijeljina, whether they perhaps have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We would be thankful to you. Can you tell us what was the year and the month when that was published?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was from 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: I just have a question for the witness. Can you recall the name of the ICRC official with whom you dealt when you are counting the number of people on the lists, the 8.000 you have just talked about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't. They rotated. But there were those from the Federation and Bijeljina. For example, Snjezana Filipkovic [phoen], she was the president of that department. There was a Ms. Melinda -- I can't recall her last name. She was from Switzerland. I can't tell you who the person in question was and who was it that I showed it to, noting that the document should be reviewed and checked for inconsistencies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have a follow-up question to that matter. If I recall correctly, you said -- yes, this it page 54, line 8: "... I handed over all the documents to Lieutenant-Colonel Miso Petricevic ...," as you are recorded to have said. When did you hand over these documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I stayed with the commission until the 30th of April, 1997, although I no longer had any contacts with the Federation Commission which had been disbanded. However, there were a number of killed in the Krajina theatre of war from our units, and I was the one who was to provide explanations to the people and comfort them. I handed over all documentation once I was finally demobilised which was on the 30th of April, 1997.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic, upon your return, when you discussed matters with those who participated with you in all the -- that -- in that whole process; for example, if you asked the interpreters, could you come up with a person's name who gave you the list, and could you tell us who it was who came to Bijeljina? Would it be possible to send those names back to us, together with the documents you may find in the ICRC office?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. All I can tell you is that I picked up the book, I underlined the problematic information, and then we no longer discussed it. I just told them that it should be improved, and that was it. The book was handed over. All I can do is to see whether there is a copy of it in the Bijeljina Red Cross office.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether the Muslims and their commissions, be it the central commissions from the Federation or the one from Tuzla, gave -- give you a definitive list of those they were looking for as missing?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are discussing the events surrounding Srebrenica, then the answer is no. There had been such lists, but, finally, this definitive list was not handed over to me. There were questions about individuals, and then I occasionally went to Batkovic to check, but as a whole, no list was received concerning such high numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have D176 shown in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is a document from the Army of B and H, their 2nd Corps command. The title is: "Chronology of events surrounding the break-through by the 28th Division of the ground forces." They forwarded it to their superior command. Could we please have page 5 in the English shown to the witness and page 4 in the Serbian version. Thank you, Aleksandar. Let's see what figures they mention. If we look at the page before you, look at the third paragraph before the mention of Lukavica. It reads: "The initial groups of refugees from Srebrenica arrived in the area of Kladanj around 9.00 p.m. and, on the 13th of July, during the day, the entire population of Srebrenica, around 22.000 of them, arrived in the general area of Dubrava airport. Some population arrived via the Baljkovica-Sapna corridor. A total of 29.336 persons expelled from the enclave were accommodated, according to the lists provided by the municipalities." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One moment, please. I don't know if you misspoke, Mr. Tolimir, or if that is a translation issue. In this paragraph, there's a reference to the 12th of July at 2100 hours, not the 13th, as you are recorded as having said. It's the 12th of July in this document. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, while we're looking at this section, and again I'm just liking at the English translation, but in the transcript General Tolimir was quoted as saying that this paragraph states that: "... the entire population of Srebrenica, around 22.000 of them, arrived in the general area of Dubrave airport." Maybe that is what it says in the original language but that is certainly not appears in the English. So I would just like some clarification so that we have an accurate transcript before us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, indeed, in the English translation it says: "The majority of them, some 22.000 to 23.000 ..."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you Mr. Thayer. I'm looking at the English translation, and the second line of the second paragraph in the English, I see the 12th of July. And on that day, 22- to 23.000 people arrived. If you look at the fifth line of that paragraph, we have a figure of 29.336, who came via Baljkovica and Sapna. Baljkovica was the place of break-through. They specify exactly how many people arrive, which is 29.336. In the break down just following this paragraph, we see further numbers. Mr. Mitrovic could look at it as well. We have the number of people accommodated in the different municipalities specified, Lukovac, Banovici, Srebrenick, Gracac, Zivinice, Kladanj, Tuzla, Kalesija and the Camp. So they provide specific figures. They mention both the 12th and the 13th of July, 1995, as the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You reminded the witness not to speak too fast. You did it yourself. And it was very difficult for the court recorder to catch everything you have said, and it was interrupted. Please put a question to the witness and that should be the last one before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic, in the paragraph I just quoted, can you also see a figure of 22- to 23.000 inhabitants, and then, toward the end of the paragraph, we have a total of 29.336 because the initial number had been joined by those who arrived via Baljkovica and Sapna. Can you tell us whether these are different routes that the groups took?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so. If this information is correct, that is how many people arrived. They also specified the routes they took. It would be useful to know exactly how many people lived in that area and compare it with this one so as to determine how are missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This it precisely what I was going to look at after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you so much. We must have our second break now, and we will resume quarter past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: As we saw in the paragraph we read out, it is stated that 29.336 inhabitants left. Then we have the breakdown by municipalities. If we look at the next page of the document, we will see that they also mentioned the number of soldiers who left. This is page 6 in the Serbian and 8 in the English. Thank you. Can you see in the eighth paragraph -- actually it begins with: "The 20th of July." It is the fifth paragraph in the English. "On the 20th of July, 1995, a tour was conducted of the facilities that would be housing the division and brigade commands and the billeting of the units began. By 2000 hours, on the 25th of July, 1995, 2.080 troops (soldiers an officers) of the 28th Division of the land forces were lined up; they are now carrying out planned tasks." By bullet points, we see the number of soldiers per brigade. If we add this figure to the previous number, it turns out that there were over 31.000 people involved, almost 31.400, who left Srebrenica. Also, according to the Muslim sources, there were additional 300 soldiers who left Srebrenica for Zepa, once Srebrenica had been overrun. If we add this to our total, it brings the number up to over 31.500.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir. Mr. Tolimir, you just mentioned additional 300 soldiers who left Srebrenica for Zepa. Where is it written in this document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I said that it was according to the Muslim sources. It is not in this document. It is in document D55, page 35, paragraph 123.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. you should now come to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic, can we see from these figures forwarded by the corps command, the 2nd Corps Command, on the basis of information about the 28th Division, how many people left Srebrenica and how many of them were registered as inhabitants and how many as soldiers?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we can see from this how many left, provided the information is correct. Because this is the information of the other side. I don't know what the number of the population was, though. This is something I can't see here, so I can't say what the difference is between the two figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We will get to that document next. I just wanted you to see that intentionally incomplete data is provided in this document. Let look at page 7 in English and 5 in the Serbian version, the last paragraph. We can see there how, in this document too, data is concealed. At the bottom of the page it says: "According to our rough assessment and knowledge, the corridor was used by a total of" -- and then there is text missing. It was intentionally deleted, that figure of how many people used the corridor. Let's look at the next page, which is page 8 in the English and 6 in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, this is quite difficult to follow. You are mixing up reference to the document and your own conclusion. Please help us but especially the witness to understand what you are putting to him. And I would like to know where it is in the English version. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. And along the same lines, I'm just trying to find out exactly where this portion is in the B/C/S. I think I can see where it is in the English, but I'd like to know exactly where in the B/C/S this portion is and whether it is indicated, as General Tolimir is suggesting, that it was deliberately omitted. I would just like to see where that line is, because I can't follow it in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, can you help us?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Yes, I can. Let's look at page 7 in the English, please, and page 5 in the Serbian. The last paragraph and the last line. It reads: "According to a rough estimate and our intelligence, a total number of" -- and now let us move onto the next page, so as not to get confused. Where we see that part of the text is missing? It is deleted, both at the end of the fifth line and the beginning of the sixth. It cannot be a coincidence. If it were deleted on only one page, it could be a coincidence. But we have text missing at the bottom of page 5 and the top of page 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we dealt with this earlier in this trial. This is your conclusion that there was something left out. But we heard other evidence that it could be a problem by making copies of the original of the document because of the size of the paper. If you want to get an answer from the witness, please put a clear question to the question and don't mix it up with your own conclusion and your own assessment. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Understood, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic, from this text, can you conclude what -- a total number of people who used the corridor by that point? Can you see that on either of the pages? Can we use the text to conclude that? And, if not, why do you think it is?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps someone could be able to deduce anything, but my conclusion would be that it was either intentional, as you say, or something is simply missing, referring to a total number of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mitrovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at the last three lines of the last page of the document in both versions. It is page 10 in the English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see it in the Serbian and in the English now. It reads: "An analysis of the events in the Srebrenica enclave and the 28th Division of the land forces break-through, put together by the 28th Division Command at the request of the 2nd Corps Commander, is entered under number, strictly confidential no 02/1-727/55 of the 24th of July, 1995, in the Corps Command records. Attachment number 34." My question is this: Having looked at the document, could we find the data that is missing so that there would be no hard feelings on either side?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if one could conclude that because I did not really study the data which you presented thoroughly, and I was not really familiar with this earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I understand you. But if a document says that it was based on a specific analysis, should the analysis then include the basic data included into this report, or memo. I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You asked to see the total number of the inhabitants of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at D117 to that purpose. Thank you. We can see here two tables showing the total numbers. It is a document from the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Srebrenica municipality, issued by the municipal TO Staff on the 11th of January, 1995: Breakdown - that's the title - of numbers of inhabitants and households per municipality; local and displaced persons; number of people who are killed; who are registered at posts; number of civilian and military casualties where the location and circumstances of death and location of burial are known, with age and gender breakdown.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So we can see the first column which says: "Population, total, 36.071." That's the total number of inhabitants in the entire Srebrenica enclave in January 1995. My question is this: Should there have been more or fewer people in July 1995, or would there be an enormous increase of inhabitants. Can you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many but, of course, between 1991 and 1995 there was some growth in terms of birth-rate but I'm not sure what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is the 11th of January, 1995. So whether in five months or six months, between January and July, the birth-rate can be enormously increased?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And then the population of municipalities is listed. Local population, Srebrenica municipality, 19.000; Bratunac municipality, 8.000; Vlasenica; Zvornik; Han Pijesak; and Visegrad municipalities; Rogatica municipality, and so on. If we see that later on we computed that it was 31.500, it was just a rough calculation, not including all the data. And if we were now to add all those that you exchanged and who figure on your list which we saw just a while ago, 171 persons, then the number would be increased by 171 persons. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, just in order for this exercise to make any real sense and have bearing relevance to the cases before this Trial Chamber, I would like to know from the Defence whether this figure of 31.500 that General Tolimir is using, I presume that is based on the document we saw a moment ago, dated 27th of July. I would like to know whether it's the Defence's position that that 31.500 figure includes people that were missing and still unaccounted for as of the date. What is the Defence's position as to that issue? I think that is a pretty important issue that seems to be absent from this series of questions that are being put to the witness. And I know I can wait until re-direct, but it is awfully complicated for me to undo this question and then reassert a hypothetical that is not my own. So I just think it would be easier if we can have an idea of what the basis of this number is and what it actually, from the Defence's position, includes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was waiting for the translation to be finished. Mr. Tolimir stated that this is his own calculation. We didn't see any document with this number of 31.500 people. It was his calculation and put to the witness. You may deal with that with the witness. He was -- this witness was not able to provide any figure on that. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. It is not my personal calculation. It is in the document D176, on those pages of the document, and I just added up the numbers which are given over ten pages. The Prosecution and the Trial Chamber can do that as well, if interested. I did not imagine the data.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, that is exactly what I just said. It was your calculation because you took a figure and then you added something. And you told us earlier that you added a different figure from a different document. So I think my summary, that this was your calculation, was correct. Please carry on and put questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic, if, in this document issued by the Army of BH which we earlier looked at, D176, includes the number of inhabitants and soldiers who left, and if there is a number in the document we are looking at now, the number of soldiers and inhabitants who were there before the fall of Srebrenica, is it then possible to calculate how many missing persons there are? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible to calculate how many missing persons there are. However, I would like to say one thing. I think that we have moved away from my testimony until now, and that now, just like in the Beara case, the Prosecution tried to drag me to Podrinje and I reacted, and, likewise, I have to react now, because I do not know enough about the situation that I'm requested to answer about at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mitrovic. I understand you. However, at the end of the examination-in-chief, you were asked whether you know what were the reasons for thousands of POWs to be transferred from Batkovic to Zvornik and so on. And later on the question was rephrased, as we can see from the record.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I then said that I did not know at all that these thousands of prisoners were transferred from Batkovici to Zvornik, and I really do not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I know that you don't know that. But do you know what was the number of Muslims from Srebrenica that you were asked about, as you were the chairman of the commission in charge of those who were at the collection centre in Batkovici where all prisoners from the zone, which includes Srebrenica, were collected? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the persons from Srebrenica, we could not even discuss that on -- about exchanges with the Tuzla commission. The state commission could do that. We were in charge of partial things that could be done. We never even received the lists of the number of persons who went missing from Srebrenica, and whatever Tuzla requested, we did. They denied that soldiers who had come there -- I went to the collection centre, and I interviewed everyone and then submitted the list to Tuzla so that one could see what unit it was, and what platoon, and what were the details, so that they could see that these were mostly soldiers, perhaps some were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mitrovic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Before the break, didn't you state that a list including 8.000 people was provided to you and that you had objections to the effect that there were many persons with the same first and last names, the place and date of birth, and so on?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The cantonal commission never provided me with a list of persons who had gone missing from Srebrenica. I simply had a chance, thanks to the good co-operation that the ICRC provided me with a list, which included some repetitions of names. How many instances there were, I couldn't tell you, but did I raise an objection that that was wrong because there were instances where information was identical. The numbers were not huge, but the document needed to be put in order because there were doubts that it could include persons still alive, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mitrovic. And can you tell us whether you know if the list was made by the representative of the ICRC who provided it to you, or whether she got it from Muslims who made it on the basis of their information and lists?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can just suppose that it was the ICRC who made it on the basis of the missing persons who were reported to them from all sides. But this is just an assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you also assume that, on the basis of that, the media and reports of various commissions, including those from Republika Srpska, mentioned the number of 7.000? Is that something you assume or is it a number which is established on the basis of certain data and information? Do you know how this number was reached?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how to tell you. I think that more investigation is still needed in order to reach a really final number. I think it's inhumane to reduce the number of victims, but it's also inhumane to increase it. In any case, there were quite sufficient numbers of casualties, even too many, and it's really bad to inflict pain on anyone in this way. There have been victims. As for the number which is mentioned, if we talk about the media, certain analysts, or, I don't know, experts, who appear, mention 3.200 as a realistic number. I just say what they are mentioning. But what the numbers really are, that's something that I would not dare to try and estimate or prognosticate, as a man.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And can you answer this question: If the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina made a report showing the number of inhabitants and soldiers who left Srebrenica, would it be correct to present that as well, and then calculate the number of persons who have gone missing on the basis of that, rather than to give approximate numbers?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. I agreed that that should be done, but also the Bosnia-Herzegovina side or the local population would not be happy about that. Then it should be investigated and it should be confirmed because it's their list, after all, and their data. Whether the data matches the actual situation, that is something that has to be investigated by those who are unhappy with the information and then either refute that or confirm it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for what you said, Mr. Mitrovic. Thank you for the knowledge you have about this issue. We will move on to other questions. Tomorrow, we will also show you a film, as we will have more time, where you will be able to see what the Muslims say and how many people perished during the break-through. My question for you now would be this: Do you know whether all who were killed during the break-through were included in the lists which the ICRC representative gave to you? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know whether they were listed. There are many things that could be discussed, whether those who were killed -- whether all those killed or perished were found, how many drowned in the Drina, when everything is ordered, investigated in the field and on the ground, and the final numbers are established, then that would represent the actual situation. And on the basis of something that appears here and there, I could not really give a judgement about the actual number and about what is true and what is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please don't get angry. I just asked you because you had seen those lists. You had them in your hands. So I just asked you for your opinion.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, but it did not say there where someone was killed, whether he was killed or not. It was just a list. It would say the list of missing persons. So I couldn't know whether he had gone missing during break-through or whether it was under other circumstances. Nothing of that was included. It was just a list of Srebrenica inhabitants who had gone missing. That is how it was formulated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked here on page 27 of today's transcript about the airport. And you answered by saying that you were twice at the airport. You've said first time was in May, and then, after that, there was another meeting. And then in the end, you said that nothing happened, but that Bulatovic [as interpreted] and Masovic would agree that five persons from each side would be exchanged. My question is this: Did you have a feeling that sometimes it was intentional not to agree about all-for-all exchanges or exchanges of great numbers of people, so that these specific persons, such as Masovic and Bulatovic, could carry out such transactions, exchanging four or five people who were paid for, as you said, 28.000 Deutschmarks. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was shameful that we should make such a trip and that then it should pass in an exchange of arguments between the two chairmen, that nothing would be agreed, that a bottle of whiskey would arrive and be emptied, and then, as if nothing had happened, the two of them would say, Look, old man - with such words - transfer these five, no problems we can do it this evening. You also transfer the other four. These were the numbers, more or less. Let me not mention the names. But there was no mention of the all-for-all exchange. What I said is true. It did happen that way. I can say another three or four sentences about that, if you want me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the president of the Muslim commission, Amor Masovic, offered an exchange to me, which I refused, I relied on the principle that exchanges should be conducted in groups, and this is what the parents of those captured at Lisace agreed with. But weapon the Tuzla Commission offered individual exchanges or groups up to five, I told the parents that if they wanted to have individual exchanges that it was up to them to determine who would be exchanged, because any splits between -- or inside a group created doubts, and these were honest people who decided to patiently wait for the whole group to be exchanged. However, there was this case I referred to, of a man from Bijeljina. His in-law provided money for him to be released, and he was released a month before the rest. And then the money had to be repaid because a debt was taken, and then the story was that he wished to end his life because he was unable to repay it, et cetera, et cetera. So that's what it boiled down to. There were expectations or lack thereof by the state commission presidents. I must say that on our side it had been a poor choice of person.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Amor Masovic receive the 28.000 German marks, or a part of, when he agreed to that exchange before everyone else was?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. But it was on our side, too. There were two such cases. Somebody who represented the parents accompanied me to an exchange, and then, all of a sudden, he offered me money for his son to be released. He did say that he knew I was an honest person who wouldn't take the money, but he said that I should give it over to the Muslims. This really angered me, and I told him the Muslims never asked for any money from me, and how would you feel if your son were released and the rest remained? So that stopped him in his tracks. There was another similar incident. It was all aimed at giving money to the other side. It wasn't attempted that I receive the money. They knew that decent people were involved in those exchanges and whenever there was any mention of money, that money was always supposed to go to the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I would kindly ask you to speak more slowly. You see how long it takes for the transcript to catch up.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We want every word of yours recorded, and the interpreters cannot speak as fast as our exchange can go. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 65 ter 5800 in e-court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see the document now. I must say, for the record, that it is a document of the Main Staff of the VRS, dated the 29th of September, 1993. It was sent to the RS government and the central commission for POW exchange, as well as civilian exchange for -- for information. It is titled: "Work of the Commission for Exchange of prisoners of war and civilians." The document was signed by General Milovanovic, Chief of the Main Staff, as we will see later when we turn to the last page. But let's first look at the contents. I just wanted to inform you of who signed this document before you begin answering my questions. I will quote from paragraph 2 which you have already read, probably. It reads: "It is a fact that your commission may not exchange prisoners of war, given that you have no prisoners of war or Muslim civilians in your zone of responsibility." I omitted to say that it was sent to the Drina Corps: "This, however, does not justify the request of some members of your commission to be granted approval by the responsible organs to have Serb civilians from territories under the Muslim control in return for money or goods." In your examination-in-chief, you also said that up to the moment when you joined the exchange process, and when Todorovic was there, there were all sorts of things taking place. It was at page 68 of the transcript. Can you tell us whether a note -- or, a document like this was inevitable, and once you took over your position, did you, as well as Todorovic, abide by the instructions issued by a higher instance, as in this case, it came from the Chief of Staff of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even without this order, when I took over the duty of the commission chairman, I conducted myself as such. First of all, I asked the chief of security to inform the corps commander that we will no longer transport packages, and at every round of talks and every exchange, there was at least a truck-load of goods that was sent to Tuzla. You mentioned superior officers. I said that I would refuse to do that and that chief of security was informed that the former chairman was paid for the transport of those packages. I wanted it to be clear that no one was going to take any money and that no packages were to be transported. Regular mail was carried, though, and all letters I received, I asked not to be sealed. We also received such shipments from Tuzla. The prisoners at Batkovic were also able to rely on the ICRC to take their mail, and we did too. So there was no trade. We tried to do it in honest terms, and that is why I always insisted on exchanging a whole group. If that could not be achieved, individual exchanges were possible, but following an approval of the president or someone higher up. If that was missing, all sorts of rumours start circulating, and then the whole issue of exchanges is doubted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mitrovic. Let's wrap this topic by me ask you this: At page 68, line 9 and onwards, you said that as of that moment, the military police took over security in Batkovic. Was the centre guarded by someone else before that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, members of the army provided security before. But they were individuals who, I believe, found a safe haven, so as to avoid being sent to the front lines. They enjoyed certain protection. I don't know who appointed them to those positions, and it is not up to me to speculate, but I didn't like that. I didn't like how they treated the prisoners because there were those who occasionally shouted, especially when I wasn't there, but it also happened even when I was there. In other words, their behaviour was incorrect, improper; although, I must say that whenever I was there, I didn't see any serious incidents such as physical mistreatment. I even interviewed the prisoners individually, without the presence of anyone from the command, to tell me whether anyone was mistreating them. I always did so individually because as a group they wouldn't dare tell me. I wanted to know whether there was anybody who mistreated them. And when cigarettes were being bought for them in town, I asked what they had -- were forced to pay for it. And I always checked what the actual price of goods and cigarettes was. The security itself boiled down to some sort of bartering, exchanges, et cetera, and, in the end, the police took it over.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all we wanted to know. And we will resume tomorrow. Have a quiet night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, will you use this document we have in front of us tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Yes, we will gladly tender it. And, in case it is not admitted, we may provide it as a reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We will tender it tomorrow, if I understand correctly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Perhaps we shouldn't waste any more time on that today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We have to adjourn for the day, and we will resume tomorrow in the afternoon, 2.15 in this courtroom. Thank you very much. We adjourn.
